docs.title: Austin
docs.text:
Austin is a Python frame stack sampler for CPython written in pure C. Samples are collected by reading the CPython interpreter virtual memory space to retrieve information about the currently running threads along with the stack of the frames that are being executed. Hence, one can use Austin to easily make powerful statistical profilers that have minimal impact on the target application and that don't require any instrumentation.

The key features of Austin are:

  • Zero instrumentation;
  • Minimal impact;
  • Fast and lightweight;
  • Time and memory profiling;
  • Built-in support for multi-process applications (e.g. mod_wsgi).
  • Support for agentic workflows, with an MCP server and a query API for coding agents.

The simplest way to turn Austin into a full-fledged profiler is to use it together with the VS Code extension or combine it with FlameGraph or Speedscope. However, Austin's binary output can be piped into any other external or custom tools for further processing. Look, for instance, at the following Python TUI

Check out A Survey of Open-Source Python Profilers by Peter Norton for a general overview of Austin. The Ecosystem page has more tool ideas and examples.

Note

This documentation is published at https://p403n1x87.github.io/austin/, with one version for each Austin minor release. If you are browsing these files on GitHub, some elements, such as admonitions like this one, won't render as intended.

docs.title: Why Austin
docs.text:
When there already are similar tools out there, it's normal to wonder why one should be interested in yet another one. So here is a list of features that currently distinguish Austin.

  • Written in pure C Austin is written in pure C code. There are no dependencies on third-party libraries except for the standard C library and the API provided by the Operating System.

  • Just a sampler Austin is just a frame stack sampler. It looks into a running Python application at regular intervals of time and dumps whatever frame stack it finds. The samples can then be analysed at a later time so that Austin can sample at rates higher than other non-C alternatives that perform some aggregations at run-time.

  • Compact output, powerful tools Austin uses the compact MOJO binary format, which can be easily parsed with the austin-python package, or converted to other popular formats. You can then go and build your own tool to analyse Austin's output. You could even make a player that replays the application execution in slow motion, so that you can see what has happened in temporal order.

  • Small size Austin compiles to a single binary executable of just a bunch of KB.

  • Easy to maintain Occasionally, the Python C API changes and Austin will need to be adjusted to new releases. However, given that Austin, like CPython, is written in C, implementing the new changes is rather straight-forward.

docs.title: Sampling Accuracy
docs.text:
Austin can sample stacks very rapidly, guaranteeing high accuracy, as well as allowing to reach very high sampling rates, if required. This makes Austin suitable for profiling applications in production with almost no compromise between accuracy and performance.

The rate of samples that cannot be collected depends on the workload: it is generally low, but it can be higher for applications whose stacks change very rapidly, e.g. with many short calls or deep recursion. See the Logging page for how to find the sampling statistics of a run.

docs.title: Support Austin
docs.text: Austin is a free and open-source project. A lot of effort goes into its development to ensure the best performance and that it stays up-to-date with the latest Python releases. If you find it useful, consider sponsoring this project, or have a look at the contributing guidelines if you want to help with the development.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Austin supports Python 3.10 through 3.15, including free-threaded builds, and has been tested on the following platforms and architectures

Linux Windows macOS x86_64 ✓ ✓ ✓ i686 ✓ armv7 ✓ arm64 ✓ ✓ ppc64le ✓

Note

Memory profiling (-m/--memory) in free-threaded Python builds is less accurate, as without the GIL there is no reliable way of attributing memory deltas to the thread that caused them.

If you are looking for support for older versions of CPython, the following table summarises the compatibility of Austin with CPython versions

CPython Versions Austin Version 2.3-2.7, 3.3-3.11 3.5 3.8-3.13 3.7 3.9-3.14 4.0 3.10-3.15, (incl. free-threaded) 4.1

Note

Austin might work with other platforms and architectures not listed above. So it is worth giving it a try even if your system is not listed. If you are looking for support for Python < 3.8, you can use Austin 3.5.

Because of platform-specific details, Austin usage may vary slightly. Below are further compatibility details to be aware of.

docs.title: On Linux
docs.text:
Austin requires the CAP_SYS_PTRACE capability to attach to an external process. This means that you will have to either use sudo when attaching to a running Python process or grant the CAP_SYS_PTRACE capability to the Austin binary with, e.g.

sudo setcap cap_sys_ptrace+ep `which austin`

To use Austin with Docker, the --cap-add SYS_PTRACE option needs to be passed when starting a container.

docs.title: On macOS
docs.text:
Due to the System Integrity Protection, introduced in macOS with El Capitan, and the Hardened Runtime, introduced in Mojave, Austin cannot profile Python processes that use an executable located in the /bin folder, or code-signed, even with sudo. This is the case for the system-provided version of Python, and the one installed with the official installers from python.org. Other installation methods, like pyenv or Anaconda or Homebrew are known to work with Austin, out of the box.

To use Austin with Python from the official installer, you could remove the signature from the binaries with

codesign --remove-signature /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/<M.m>/bin/python3
codesign --remove-signature /Library/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/<M.m>/Resources/Python.app/Contents/MacOS/Python

Alternatively, you could self-sign the Austin binary with the Debugging Tool Entitlement, as done for debugging tools like GDB. However, this method has not been tested.

Tip

Austin requires the use of sudo to work on macOS. To avoid having to type the password every time you use Austin, consider adding a rule to the sudoers file, e.g.

yourusername  ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/austin

docs.title: Ecosystem
docs.text: Austin's MOJO output can be consumed by a number of tools, or by your own, with the help of the austin-python package.

docs.title: Agentic Workflows
docs.text:
Coding agents can profile Python code with Austin and reason about the results on their own. There are two ways to give an agent access to Austin profiles:

VS Code MCP server austin-query Best for Interactive sessions in the editor, where you and the agent look at the same flame graph Headless use: terminal agents, scripts and CI Requires The Austin VS Code extension The austin-python package Agents GitHub Copilot out of the box, or any MCP client, like Claude Code or Cursor Any agent that can run shell commands Output Structured MCP tool results, plus flame graph actions Text tables, or JSON with --json

In both cases, the agent works from the same questions you would ask: what the hottest functions are, who calls them, which call stacks are the heaviest, how busy the garbage collector is, and what each asyncio task was doing.

docs.title: IDE Extensions
docs.text:
It is easy to write your own extension for your favourite text editor. This, for example, is a demo of the Visual Studio Code extension that highlights the most hit lines of code straight into the editor

The extension opens .mojo files directly, and renders interactive flame graphs, source-level annotations and thread breakdowns, with support for the asyncio task view of profiles collected on CPython 3.14 or later.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
The Austin VS Code extension comes with an MCP server that exposes the profile loaded in the editor to AI agents. The server starts automatically when the extension activates, and offers two kinds of tools.

The data tools let the agent read the loaded profile:

Tool Description get_top Top functions, sorted by own time get_call_stacks Process, thread and function call-stack tree, with an optional threshold to prune branches that contribute little get_metadata Source file, sampling mode, interval and total sample count get_gc_data Per-thread garbage collector time, and the functions on the stack during collections get_task_traces asyncio task trees, with each task's coroutine, location, running and total time

The action tools let the agent show its findings in the flame graph:

Tool Description load_profile Load a profile file and open it in the flame graph view focus_flamegraph Zoom the flame graph to a call-stack or task node search_flamegraph Highlight every frame whose function name contains a term

This way, an agent can profile your code, load the result, explain where the time goes, and point you to the relevant part of the flame graph, all within the same chat session.

In VS Code, the server is registered with the built-in MCP client, and the tools are available in GitHub Copilot's agent mode with no configuration. For other agents with their own MCP client, like Claude Code or Cursor, run the Austin: Generate .mcp.json command from the Command Palette. This writes a .mcp.json file to the workspace root that points the agent to the server. To share this file with your team, set the austin.mcp.port setting to a fixed port before generating it. The extension's documentation has all the details.

docs.title: Querying Profiles
docs.text:
The austin.query module of the austin-python package answers the most common questions about a profile, like which functions are the hottest, what the sampled stacks are, or who calls a given function:

from austin.query import ProfileQuery

q = ProfileQuery.from_file("profile.mojo")

print(q.top(10))                       # hottest functions
print(q.callers("db.py:execute"))      # who calls execute
print(q.filter(thread="main").tree())  # call tree of the main thread

Every result renders as a text table when printed, and can be converted to JSON-ready data with to_dict(). For asyncio profiles (CPython 3.14 or later), q.tasks() shows the task trees, q.task_stacks("worker-0") where a task was running and awaiting, and q.filter(task="worker-0") narrows any query down to the samples in which a task was running.

The same queries are available from the command line with the austin-query tool, which makes them easy to use for any agent that can run shell commands. A typical session goes from an overview of the profile down to the code that needs attention:

austin-query profile.mojo summary          # mode, metrics and threads
austin-query profile.mojo top -n 20        # hottest functions
austin-query profile.mojo callers execute  # who calls a hot function
austin-query profile.mojo stacks -n 5      # heaviest full stacks
austin-query profile.mojo tasks            # asyncio task trees

Add --json to any command for machine-readable output. Run austin-query --help for the syntax that selects functions and tasks, and for the suggested workflow. Pointing an agent to austin-query --help is usually all it takes for it to profile and analyse your code on its own:

austin -o profile.mojo python myscript.py
austin-query profile.mojo top -n 10 --json

Note

The query API and the austin-query tool are available since austin-python 2.5.0. Install or upgrade with pip install -U austin-python.

docs.title: Austin TUI
docs.text:
The Austin TUI is a text-based user interface for Austin that gives you a top-like view of what is currently running inside a Python application. It is most useful for scripts that have long-running procedures as you can see where execution is at without tracing instructions in your code. You can also save the collected data from within the TUI and feed it to Flame Graph for visualisation, or convert it to the pprof format.

If you want to give it a go you can install it using pip with

pip install austin-tui --upgrade

and run it with

austin-tui [OPTION...] command [ARG...]

with the same command line as Austin. Please note that the austin binary should be available from within the PATH environment variable in order for the TUI to work.

Important

The TUI is based on python-curses. The version included with the standard Windows installations of Python is broken so it won't work out of the box. A solution is to install the wheel of the port to Windows from this page. Wheel files can be installed directly with pip, as described in the linked page.

docs.title: Austin Web
docs.text:
Austin Web is a web application that wraps around Austin. At its core, Austin Web is based on d3-flame-graph to display a live flame graph in the browser, that refreshes every 3 seconds with newly collected samples. Austin Web can also be used for remote profiling by setting the --host and --port options.

If you want to give it a go you can install it using pip with

pip install austin-web --upgrade

and run it with

austin-web [OPTION...] command [ARG...]

with the same command line as Austin. This starts a simple HTTP server that serves on localhost by default. When no explicit port is given, Austin Web will use an ephemeral one.

Please note that the austin binary should be available from within the PATH environment variable in order for Austin Web to work.

docs.title: Speedscope
docs.text:
Austin's MOJO output can be converted to the Speedscope JSON format with the austin2speedscope utility that comes with the austin-python package.

If you want to give it a go you can install it using pip with

pip install austin-python --upgrade

and run it with

austin2speedscope [-h] [--indent INDENT] [-V] input output

where input is a file containing the output from Austin and output is the name of the JSON file to use to save the result of the conversion, ready to be used on Speedscope.

docs.title: Google pprof
docs.text:
Austin's format can also be converted to the Google pprof format using the austin2pprof utility that comes with austin-python. If you want to give it a go you can install it using pip with

pip install austin-python --upgrade

and run it with

austin2pprof [-h] [-V] input output

where input is a file containing the output from Austin and output is the name of the protobuf file to use to save the result of the conversion, ready to be used with Google's pprof tools.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
Besides sampling the Python stacks of a process to measure where time is spent, Austin can collect a range of other information, often from the same run.

Feature Option Description Multi-process applications -C/--children Sample the child processes of the target too Sub-interpreters Sample all the sub-interpreters of each process Thread names Report threads by their threading name Where? -w/--where Print the current stacks of a running process Memory and full metrics -m/--memory, -f/--full Sample memory deltas, or time, memory and CPU state in one run Garbage collector -g/--gc Mark the samples taken while the GC is collecting Asyncio support Track the asyncio task graph on CPython 3.14+ Native frame stack -n/--native Collect native call stacks alongside the Python ones Column-level locations Report column-level location information on CPython 3.11+

docs.title: Multi-process Applications
docs.text:
Austin can be told to profile multi-process applications with the -C or --children switch. This way Austin will look for new children of the parent process.

See the examples for how to profile a multi-process application such as an Apache2 WSGI server.

docs.title: Sub-interpreters
docs.text:
Austin has support for Python applications that make use of sub-interpreters. This means that Austin will sample all the sub-interpreters that are running within each process making up the Python application.

Since Austin 3.6.0.

docs.title: Thread Names
docs.text:
Austin reports Python threads by the name they have in the threading module (e.g. MainThread), whenever this can be resolved. Threads that are not known to the threading module, like those created by native extensions, are reported by their thread ID.

Since Austin 4.1.0.

docs.title: Where?
docs.text:
If you are only interested in what is currently happening inside a Python process, you can have a quick overview printed on the terminal with the -w/--where option. This takes the PID of the process whose threads you want to inspect, e.g.

sudo austin -w `pgrep -f my-running-python-app`

Below is an example of what the output looks like

This works with the -C/--children option too. The emojis to the left indicate whether the thread is active or sleeping and whether the process is a child or not.

The where option also supports native mode and renders the asyncio task graph of applications running on CPython 3.14 or later.

Since Austin 3.3.0.

docs.title: Memory and Full Metrics
docs.text:
When profiling in memory mode with the -m or --memory switch, the metric value associated with each stack is the memory delta between samples, measured in bytes. In full mode (-f or --full switches), each sample will include both a time and memory metric, plus the information of whether the stack was on CPU. This is useful if you want to collect wall-time/CPU-time and memory profiles in a single run.

Note

The reported memory allocations and deallocations are obtained by computing resident memory deltas between samples. Hence these values give an idea of how much physical memory is being requested/released.

Note

Memory profiling in free-threaded Python builds is less accurate, as without the GIL there is no reliable way of attributing memory deltas to the thread that caused them.

docs.title: Garbage Collector Sampling
docs.text:
Austin can sample the Python garbage collector state. If the -g/--gc option is passed, Austin will mark each collected sample that was taken while the garbage collector was collecting. This gives you a measure of how busy the Python GC is during a run.

Since Austin 3.1.0.

docs.title: Asyncio Support
docs.text:
For applications running on CPython 3.14 or later, Austin can also track the asyncio task graph: each event loop's own tasks, the coroutine chain each task is currently suspended at or executing, and the await relationships between tasks.

When profiling, the collected samples are attributed to the task that is running on the sampled thread, and the stacks of the suspended tasks are reported together with the await relationships between tasks. This allows tools like the Austin VS Code extension to reconstruct a task-level view of the application that also accounts for the time tasks spend waiting. The MOJO format page describes how this information is encoded.

With -w/--where, tasks are rendered as a tree nested under the thread whose event loop owns them, so you can see at a glance which coroutines each task is waiting on. Tasks whose owning thread has since terminated are listed separately as orphaned.

Note

Asyncio task tracking is not currently available in native mode (-n/--native).

Since Austin 4.1.0.

docs.title: Native Frame Stack
docs.text:
If you want observability into the native frame stacks, you can pass the -n/--native option to collect native call stacks alongside the Python ones, e.g.

austin -n -i 1ms -o profile.mojo python myscript.py

Native frames are interleaved with the Python frames that they belong to, and are reported with the path of the binary they come from and the name of the function, resolved from the binary's symbol table. In native mode, Austin also samples threads that are not running any Python code, like those created by native extensions, to give a more comprehensive view of what is running within a Python process. The where option also supports native mode.

Native mode is available on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64), macOS and Windows (x86_64), and requires no additional dependencies. On any other platforms or architectures, the option is ignored with a warning.

Warning

To capture a consistent native stack, Austin needs to briefly suspend each thread while sampling it. Therefore, the impact on the tracee is no longer minimal and it becomes higher at smaller sampling intervals. For this reason, consider using larger sampling intervals in native mode (e.g. -i 1ms or higher), and avoid using it in production environments.

Note

On Windows, symbols are resolved with DbgHelp. For accurate function names, make sure that the PDB files of the binaries of interest are available, e.g. by setting the _NT_SYMBOL_PATH environment variable to point to a symbol server, as described in the Windows documentation.

Since Austin 4.1.0.

docs.title: The austinp variant
docs.text:
On Linux, the austinp variant of austin provides an alternative native mode, which also supports architectures other than x86_64 and aarch64, as well as the sampling of kernel call stacks. It can be obtained by compiling the source with -DAUSTINP, or from the released binaries.

austinp makes use of ptrace to halt the application and grab a snapshot of the call stack with libunwind. If you are compiling austinp from sources make sure that you have the development version of the libunwind library available on your system, for example on Ubuntu,

sudo apt install libunwind-dev binutils-dev

and compile with

gcc -O3 -Os -Wall -pthread src/*.c -DAUSTINP -lunwind-ptrace -lunwind-generic -lbfd -o src/austinp

then use as per normal. The extra -k/--kernel option is available with austinp which allows sampling kernel call stacks as well.

Warning

Since austinp uses ptrace, the impact on the tracee is no longer minimal and it becomes higher at smaller sampling intervals. Therefore the use of austinp is not recommended in production environments. For this reason, the default sampling interval for austinp is 10 milliseconds.

The austinp-resolve tool from the austin-python Python package can be used to resolve the VM addresses to source and line numbers, provided that the referenced binaries have DWARF debug symbols. Internally, the tool uses addr2line(1) to determine the source name and line number given an address, when possible.

Note

Whilst austinp comes with a stripped-down implementation of addr2line, it is only used for the "where" option, as resolving symbols at runtime is expensive. This is to minimise the impact of austinp on the tracee, increase accuracy and maximise the sampling rate.

The where option is also available for the austinp variant and will show both native and Python frames. Highlighting helps tell frames apart. The -k option outputs Linux kernel frames too, as shown in this example

Note

If you have installed Austin from the Snap Store, the austinp executable will be available as austin.p from the command line.

docs.title: Column-level Location Information
docs.text:
Since Python 3.11, code objects carry finer-grained location information at the column level. When using the binary MOJO format, Austin can extract this extra location information when profiling code running with versions of the interpreter that expose this data.

Since Austin 3.5.0.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Austin is available to install from PyPI and from the major software repositories of the most popular platforms. Check out the latest release page for pre-compiled binaries and installation packages.

On all supported platforms and architectures, Austin can be installed from PyPI with pip or pipx via the commands

pip install austin-dist

or

pipx install austin-dist

On Linux, it can be installed using autotools or as a snap from the Snap Store. The latter will automatically perform the steps of the autotools method with a single command. On distributions derived from Debian, Austin can be installed from the official repositories with apt. Anaconda users can install Austin from Conda Forge.

On Windows, Austin can be easily installed from the command line using either Chocolatey or Scoop. Alternatively, you can download the installer from the latest release page.

On macOS, Austin can be easily installed from the command line using Homebrew. Anaconda users can install Austin from Conda Forge.

For any other platforms, compiling Austin from sources is as easy as cloning the repository and running the C compiler. The Releases page has many pre-compiled binaries that are ready to be uncompressed and used.

docs.title: With autotools
docs.text:
Installing Austin using autotools amounts to the usual ./configure, make and make install finger gymnastic. The only dependency is the standard C library. Before proceeding with the steps below, make sure that the autotools are installed on your system. Refer to your distro's documentation for details on how to do so.

git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/P403n1x87/austin.git && cd austin
autoreconf --install
./configure
make
make install

Note

Some Linux distributions, like Manjaro, might require the execution of automake --add-missing before ./configure.

Alternatively, sources can be compiled with just a C compiler (see below).

docs.title: From the Snap Store
docs.text:
Austin can be installed on many major Linux distributions from the Snap Store with the following command

sudo snap install austin --classic

docs.title: On Debian and Derivatives
docs.text:
On March 30 2019 Austin was accepted into the official Debian repositories and can therefore be installed with the apt utility.

sudo apt update -y && sudo apt install austin -y

docs.title: On macOS
docs.text:
Austin can be installed on macOS using Homebrew:

brew install austin

docs.title: From Chocolatey
docs.text:
To install Austin from Chocolatey, run the following command from the command line or from PowerShell

choco install austin

To upgrade run the following command from the command line or from PowerShell:

choco upgrade austin

docs.title: From Scoop
docs.text:
To install Austin using Scoop, run the following command from the command line or PowerShell

scoop install austin

To upgrade run the following command from the command line or PowerShell:

scoop update

docs.title: From Conda Forge
docs.text:
Anaconda users on Linux and macOS can install Austin from Conda Forge with the command

conda install -c conda-forge austin

docs.title: From Sources without autotools
docs.text:
To install Austin from sources using the GNU C compiler, without autotools, clone the repository with

git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/P403n1x87/austin.git

On Linux, one can then use the command

gcc -O3 -Os -Wall -pthread src/*.c -o src/austin

whereas on macOS it is enough to run

gcc -O3 -Os -Wall src/*.c -o src/austin

On Windows, the -lpsapi -lntdll -ldbghelp switches are needed

gcc -O3 -Os -Wall -lpsapi -lntdll -ldbghelp src/*.c -o src/austin

Add -DDEBUG if you need a more verbose log. This is useful if you encounter a bug with Austin and you want to report it.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Austin uses syslog on Linux and macOS, and %TEMP%\austin.log on Windows for log messages, so make sure to watch these to get execution details and statistics. Bad frames are output together with the other frames. The error rate depends on the workload: it is generally low, but it can be higher for applications whose stacks change very rapidly, e.g. with many short calls or deep recursion.

Logging can be disabled using environment variables.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Usage: austin [-CcfgmnP?V] [-x n_sec] [-i n_us] [-o FILE] [-p PID] [-t n_ms]
               [-w PID] command [ARG...]

Austin is a frame stack sampler for CPython that is used to extract profiling
data out of a running Python process (and all its children, if required) that
requires no instrumentation and has practically no impact on the tracee.

Options:
  -C, --children              Attach to child processes.
  -c, --cpu                   Sample on-CPU stacks only.
  -x, --exposure <n_sec>      Sample for n_sec seconds only.
  -f, --full                  Produce the full set of metrics (time +mem -mem).
  -g, --gc                    Sample the garbage collector state.
  -i, --interval <n_us>       Sampling interval in microseconds (default is
                              100). Accepted units: s, ms, us.
  -m, --memory                Profile memory usage.
  -n, --native                Collect native call stacks alongside Python
                              stacks.
  -o, --output <FILE>         Specify an output file for the collected samples.
  -p, --pid <PID>             Attach to the process with the given PID.
  -P, --pipe                  Pipe mode. Use when piping Austin output.
  -t, --timeout <n_ms>        Start up wait time in milliseconds (default is
                              3000). Accepted units: s, ms.
  -w, --where <PID>           Dump the stacks of all the threads within the
                              process with the given PID.
  -?, --help                  Give this help list.
      --usage                 Give a short usage message.
  -V, --version               Print program version.

Report bugs at https://github.com/P403n1x87/austin/issues

Austin generates binary output in the MOJO format. This is a compact binary representation of the collected data that can be processed by the mojo2austin tool that comes with the austin-python Python package to produce the more commonly used collapsed stack format. The MOJO format can also be converted to the Speedscope JSON format using the austin2speedscope tool that also comes with the austin-python Python package.

Tip

The recommended way to visualise Austin profiles is with the Austin VS Code extension. It opens .mojo files directly and renders interactive flame graphs, source-level annotations, and thread breakdowns without any extra conversion steps. The extension also ships with an MCP server that lets coding agents query profiling data autonomously, and the austin-query tool lets them query profiles from the command line.

If you prefer command-line tools such as Brendan Gregg's flamegraph.pl to generate flame graph visualisations, you first need to convert Austin's MOJO output to collapsed stack format with the mojo2austin utility from the austin-python package:

pip install austin-python
mojo2austin profile.mojo /dev/stdout | flamegraph.pl > profile.svg

Open profile.svg in a browser to explore the interactive flame graph.

Note

Austin writes binary MOJO data to stdout by default, so piping Austin's output directly into flamegraph.pl will not work. Always save to a file first (with -o profile.mojo or output redirection) and then convert with mojo2austin.

Important

If you are running Austin directly in a terminal, make sure to either redirect the output to a file or give a destination file with the -o/--output option to avoid the terminal being flooded with binary data.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
To profile a Python script, run Austin with the command

austin -o profile.mojo python myscript.py

To profile a running Python application, attach Austin to it with the -p/--pid option, e.g.

austin -o profile.mojo -p <pid>

where <pid> is the process ID of the running Python application you want to profile. If you also want to profile the child processes of the target application, add the -C/--children option to the command line:

austin -o profile.mojo -Cp <pid>

For example, to profile an Apache2 WSGI application, one can attach Austin to the web server with

austin -Cp `pgrep apache2 | head -n 1` > profile.mojo

Any child processes will be automatically detected as they are created and Austin will sample them too.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Some behaviour of Austin can be configured via environment variables.

Variable Effect AUSTIN_NO_LOGGING Disables all log messages (since Austin 3.4.0). AUSTIN_PAGE_SIZE_CAP Cap the page size used to perform remote reads (since Austin 4.0.0).

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text: All the above Austin options and arguments are summarised in a cheat sheet, available in the SVG, PDF and PNG formats.

docs.title: The MOJO File Format
docs.text: This page describes Austin's MOJO binary file format for version 4. At the high level, it consists of a stream of events that correspond to the various parts of Austin's default output format. Each MOJO file has a header with a magic sequence of bytes and a version number.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text: There are only two fundamental data types used by the MOJO format: strings and varints. A string is a null-terminated sequence of bytes. A varint is an integer of variable size which is encoded as follows: the most significant bit of each byte determines whether the next byte is part of the number. The second most significant bit of the first byte is the sign bit. Hence, only the last 6 least significant bits of the first byte contribute to the value of the integer, whereas for each of the subsequent bytes, the number of bits is 7. For example, the byte sequence C3 02 encodes the integer -131.

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
A MOJO file starts with the byte sequence

Byte 0 .. 2 Byte 3 .. MOJ version varint

that is, the byte sequence MOJ followed by the varint encoding of the format version. The initial version is 1. The latest version is 4.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Each event has the following structure

Byte 0 Byte 1 .. n Event ID Event data

Note that some events might not have any additional event data. The currently supported event IDs are listed in the following table.

Event ID Name Event Data Description 0 Reserved. 1 Metadata key: string, value: string Metadata key-value pair, e.g. Austin version, detected Python version, sampling metrics etc... . 2 Stack pid: varint, iid: varint, thread: string This signals the beginning of a sample. The event data includes the PID, the interpreter ID, and the thread identifier. The thread identifier is the name of the thread, as known to the threading module (e.g. MainThread), when it can be resolved, or the thread ID otherwise. Every new stack event signals the end of the previous sample (if any) and the beginning of a new one. 3 Frame key: varint, filename_key: varint, scope_key: varint, line: varint, line_end: varint, column: varint, column_end: varint This event carries information about a frame. The event data consists of the frame key identifier, two string references for the file path and the function name respectively, and the location information. The location information consists of 4 numbers: the start and end line, and the start and end column. A value of 0 indicates that no information is available for that location value. See below for how native frames are encoded. 4 Invalid frame Emitted when an invalid frame is detected. Not emitted since Austin 4.0, but kept for compatibility with older versions. 5 Frame reference frame_key: varint A reference to a frame by key identifier. These events define the actual frame content of frame stacks. 6 Kernel frame symbol: string Emitted by the austinp variant to report a kernel frame. The event data is a single string with the name of the kernel symbol. 7 Garbage collector Emitted if the garbage collector is running while sampling with the garbage collector option. 8 Idle stack Emitted if the stack is idle (only in full mode). 9 Time metric value: varint A time delta in microseconds 10 Memory metric value: varint A memory delta in bytes. 11 String event key: varint, value: string This is a pair of key followed by a literal string. Used to provide a mapping between a string and a string reference, which is used to reduce redundancy. 12 String reference string_key: varint A reference to a string by key. 13 Stack repeat The Python frames of the current sample are the same as those of the previous sample of the same thread (same PID and thread identifier). See below for details. 14 Task stack task_id: varint, name_key: varint, frame_count: varint Reports the current coroutine stack of an asyncio task. The event data consists of the task identifier, a string reference to the task name (0 if not available), and the number of frame references that follow and make up the task stack. See below for details. 15 Task waiter task_id: varint, waiter_id: varint An edge of the asyncio task graph: the task with identifier task_id is being awaited by the task with identifier waiter_id. A waiter_id of 0 means that the task has no waiters. See below for details. 16 Running task task_id: varint The asyncio task that the thread of the current sample is running. See below for details.

docs.title: Samples
docs.text:
A sample is made of the following sequence of events, in this order

  1. a Stack event;
  2. optionally, any asyncio task events (Task stack, Task waiter, Running task) for the tasks owned by the thread of the sample;
  3. optionally, a Stack repeat event;
  4. the Frame reference events of the sample, from the outermost to the innermost frame, followed by any Kernel frame events;
  5. optionally, a Garbage collector event;
  6. the metric events: a Time metric or a Memory metric event, or, in full mode, a Time metric event, an optional Idle stack event and a Memory metric event.

Frame and String events, that define new frames and strings, can appear anywhere in the stream before they are first referenced. Metadata events are mostly emitted at the beginning and at the end of the stream, outside of any sample.

docs.title: Stack repeats
docs.text:
To reduce the cost of sampling, and the size of MOJO files, Austin can detect when the Python frames of a thread are the same as those of the previous sample of the same thread. In this case, a Stack repeat event is emitted instead of the frame references of the Python stack. The frames of the sample are then those of the previous sample of the same thread, followed by the Frame reference events that come after the Stack repeat event, if any.

In native mode, the native frames that are above the innermost Python frame might change between samples, even when the Python stack is the same. Therefore, the trailing native frames of the previous sample must be dropped before appending the frames that come after the Stack repeat event. Native frames are those whose file name does not end in .py and that are not of the form <...>.

docs.title: Asyncio tasks
docs.text:
For applications running on CPython 3.14 and later, Austin reports information about the asyncio tasks owned by each thread. Asyncio task events are emitted within the sample of the thread that owns the tasks, between the Stack event and the frame references of the sample. They are not available in native mode.

Tasks are identified by a sequential number assigned by Austin, and not by their memory address, so that a new task allocated at the same address as a task that has gone away is not confused with it. The identifier 0 is never assigned to a task.

Task stack events are emitted for a suspended task only when its position has changed since the last time it was reported. A task that is executing when the sample is taken is reported in every such sample, with the portion of the thread stack that belongs to the task. The event is followed by exactly frame_count Frame reference events that make up the coroutine stack of the task, from the outermost to the innermost frame; only Frame reference events count towards frame_count. A Task stack event with a frame_count of 0 signals that the task has gone away. Task stack events carry no metrics: the time a task spends at a position is the time of the samples of its thread while the task is at that position.

Task waiter events describe the await relationships between tasks. They are emitted whenever the set of waiters of a task changes, as a run of consecutive events with the same task_id, one for each direct waiter. The run replaces the whole set of known waiters of the task. A single event with a waiter_id of 0 means that the task has no waiters anymore.

Running task events report the task that the thread of the sample is running. The task is always reported by a Task stack event before it is referenced. When this event is present, the metrics of the sample belong to the running task, at its latest reported position, and the frame references of the sample are those of the thread that are outside the task's own coroutine stack (e.g. the event loop frames). When the event is absent, the sample belongs to the thread alone.

docs.title: Native frames
docs.text: When Austin runs in native mode (-n/--native, or with the austinp variant), native frames are reported with Frame events too, interleaved with the Python frames that they belong to. For a native frame, the file name is the path of the binary that contains the code (or native@<address> if the binary cannot be determined) and the scope is the name of the function. The location fields are set to 0, except for the austinp variant, where the line field carries the offset of the instruction within the function.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Reference events, like frame and string events, make use of varint key. To further reduce the size of MOJO files, these keys are such that their varint-encoded value is at most 4 bytes, for a total of 2^27 (~134 M) possible values.

The string key 1 is reserved for the string <unknown>, which is used, e.g., for the scope of a native frame whose function name cannot be resolved. No String event is emitted for it.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• Added the Stack repeat event.
  • Added the Task stack, Task waiter and Running task events for asyncio support.
  • The thread identifier of the Stack event is now the name of the thread, when it can be resolved.
  • The string key 1 is now reserved for the <unknown> string.
